fact: A match between Tom Allen and Bill Ryall fell through about 1866 over the choice of a battle ground.
In 1867 Joe Goss offered Tom Allen a rematch, which Allen refused, even though Goss offered to increase the stakes.
In March 1868 Mike McCoole proposed a fight with Tom Allen after withdrawing from their match, and Allen intended to accept McCoole's proposal.
Tom Allen issued a boasting challenge that he could whip any man in the world, and Jem Mace accepted it.
Tom Allen and Charley Gallagher agreed to a London prize ring fight for 23 February 1869, with articles drawn up and forfeits posted.
Tom Allen said he would fight any man in the country who disputed his claim, for any purse the challenger named.
In late February 1869 Tom Allen challenged Charley Gallagher to a rematch.
Tom Allen kept demanding another fight, saying he was able and willing to fight any man in America.
On 6 March 1869 at a Chestnut Street saloon, Tom Allen and Mike McCoole agreed to a $1,000 wager, with a $50 forfeit that Allen covered.
On 8 March 1869 Tom Allen and Mike McCoole agreed to withdraw the stakes on their match and postpone the fight.
In March 1869 Tom Allen challenged Mike McCoole to fight for $2,500 a side within three months, and Billy Carroll proposed London prize ring terms for the match.
Patsy Reardon challenged Tom Allen in March 1869 to a bout in the twenty-four-foot arena, and Allen answered with a counter-challenge with provisos.
Tom Allen and Mike McCoole signed articles for a London prize ring fight for $1,000 a side, after Allen agreed to a long delay so McCoole could train.
In June 1869 Tom Allen refused a return match with Mike McCoole near St. Louis, and the two exchanged challenges while a renewal was being worked on.
Tom Allen had an appointment to meet Mike McCoole to make arrangements for another fight in June 1869, but did not come.
Tom Allen offered to fight Charley Gallagher for $2,500 to $1,500, and a meeting was fixed for 17 August 1869.
Tom Allen said he was willing to fight any man in America for a purse of $1,000 to $5,000.
Ben Hogan of Titusville, Pennsylvania, challenged Tom Allen to a London prize ring fight for $1,000 and the boat money, to take place in Canada West three months after articles are signed.
Tom Allen said he would meet Charley Gallagher at any place Gallagher named to draw up articles, if Gallagher covered a $200 deposit.
Tom Allen challenged Charley Gallagher to fight for $500, apart from his McCoole match, and deposited $100 with his backer Billy Carroll for Gallagher to cover.
Tom Allen and Charley Gallagher made a match for $500 a side and the excursion money, to be fought on August 17 within fifty miles of St. Louis.
Ben Hogan arrived in St. Louis and said he was willing to fight Tom Allen.
Patsey Reardon published a challenge in a St. Louis paper to fight Tom Allen.
Jim Coyne challenged Ben Hogan to fight four weeks after the Allen and Gallagher fight, for $500 or $1,000 a side.

After Allen and Gallagher's fight, Gallagher proposed a return fight for the same stakes plus about $1,000 a side, and Tom Allen accepted it around August 20, 1869; Allen was to name a place within fifty miles of Cincinnati and meet Gallagher on Saturday afternoon to draw up articles.
Joe Wormald wrote to Tom Allen asking him to arrange the preliminaries of a match with Ned O'Baldwin for $5,000 a side.
Jack Looney offered to back Charley Gallagher against Tom Allen for any amount once Gallagher recovered.
A deposit for the Mike McCoole and Tom Allen match was put up at Allen's saloon on the night of October 9, 1869.
Tom Allen and Mike McCoole negotiated a match for the championship of America, set for November 10, 1869, and it did not take place.
Tom Allen announced he would fight any man in America for $500 to $10,000 in a square stand-up fight under London prize ring rules.
Tom Allen offered to meet Joe Coburn in the ring anywhere in Wyoming Territory, whom he called the leading scientific pugilist in the United States.
Tom Allen, through Billy Carroll, offered to fight Jem Mace for $2,500 a side, six months from signing articles, and in late December forwarded forfeit money accepting Mace's challenge.
Tom Allen apparently accepted Joe Coburn's challenge to fight for $10,000, although the report is garbled.

Tom Allen and Jem Mace each deposited $500 with a stakeholder, and Mace offered to meet Allen in New York and pay half his expenses there, after the Clipper reported that Mace accepted Allen's challenge.
Tom Allen and Jem Mace agreed in January 1870 to a fight for the championship, and articles were drawn up.
Tom Allen declined Joe Coburn's January 1870 challenge to fight for $5,000 or $10,000, saying he would not fight Coburn until after his contest with Jem Mace, expected in July 1870.
Jem Mace wrote in a March 1870 card that he would only whip Tom Allen for the reputation and battle-money of their meeting, with no international character.
In May 1870 Tom Allen challenged all professional bruisers except Mace and Heenan to fight him, and was particularly anxious that Joe Coburn accept.
Tom Allen and Mike McCoole were matched for the championship in summer 1870 with $1,000 deposited, but the second deposit was not paid.
A match between Tom Allen and Jem Mace was set for July 5, 1870, to be fought within fifty miles of Cincinnati for $2,500 a side.
Allen said no match had been made with Joe Goss, dismissing New York rumours of a $1,000-a-side match as moonshine.
In July 1870 Tom Allen sent the New York Clipper a challenge to fight any man in America for $2,500 or $5,000 a side, Joe Coburn preferred.

Tom Allen and James C. Gallagher signed articles at Hennessy's saloon on September 19, 1870 for a $1,500 match, with deposits paid through October. In November Gallagher proposed Louisiana, Kansas, Arkansas or Kentucky as the venue, and Allen said he would fight in any of them.
Jack Leoney offered $5,000 to back Tom Allen in a match in 1871.
In a letter dated January 1871 from St. Louis, Tom Allen said he had challenged Joe Coburn ten times and that Coburn never answered.
Allen offered Joe Coburn $200 to withdraw from his match with Jem Mace, and offered to stake $3,000 for a fight with Coburn on April 11, 1871, about fifty miles from Detroit.
A New York dispatch of May 14, 1871 said Tom Allen offered to fight Joe Coburn or Ned O'Baldwin, and Allen denied the dispatch on May 16.
In early 1872 Tom Allen and Mike McCoole were negotiating a match, with Billy Carroll offering to back McCoole and Allen putting up $500 to meet him.
A match between Tom Kelly and Tom Allen was rumoured in late November 1872, with friends of Kelly offering $500 or more to back him if Allen could be brought down to Kelly's weight.
Tom Allen offered to fight Mike McCoole at any time for any amount and put $500 on the counter as a forfeit, but McCoole did not respond.
Tom Allen and Mike McCoole signed articles in May 1873 for a London prize ring fight, with deposits posted through the summer and the fight set for 23 September 1873.
Tom Allen and Ben Hogan signed articles on 25 September 1873 for a fight under the new London prize ring rules.
In October 1873 Tom Allen challenged Joe Coburn to a fight for $500 to $5,000 and offered a forfeit.
On 23 and 24 October 1873 Tom Allen offered to fight any man in the world and any Irish-American, and offered a standing bet of his money and property.
On 28 and 29 November 1873 Tom Allen challenged Ben Hogan to fight in Canada within weeks, and Hogan declined for now because of illness.
In January 1874 Tom Allen challenged Jem Mace, Joe Coburn or any other man to a London prize ring fight for $1,000 to $5,000 a side.
In February 1874 Jem Mace was reported willing to accept Tom Allen's challenge, with a forfeit required.
In November 1874 Tom Allen denied a New York report of a challenge to Bell's Life and said his earlier challenge had never been accepted.
After the failed Rooke match, Tom Allen issued an open challenge to any man in the country for $2,500 to $5,000 a side and the championship of the world.

George Rooke challenged Tom Allen in early 1875 to fight for the American championship at $2,500 a side; Arthur Chambers accepted for Allen, the two met at Harry Hill's in New York on February 16, 1875 to discuss stakes, and Harry Hill held a $500 deposit in March.
Ben Hogan challenged Tom Allen to fight for $2,500 a side in April 1875, and Allen accepted by letter to Sam French, with a $250 deposit sent to bind the match.

In June 1875 Arthur Chambers sent George Rooke articles for a fight within fifty miles of Detroit at $1,000 a side, after Allen telegraphed Philadelphia, and Rooke's backer Muldoon and Rooke himself also offered terms for a match with Allen.
Talk of a match between Tom Allen and Ned O'Baldwin arose in late June 1875, and efforts to arrange it went on for three months.
Teddy Neary, brother of Fiddler Neary, was eager to fight George Rooke and would be matched against him if Allen's challenge came to nothing.
A New York report in July 1875 said Tom Allen had challenged Jem Mace and that Mace had accepted; the paper said the report was a scheme and not true.

Jem Mace challenged Tom Allen by letter from London dated October 27, 1875, and Allen's replies from November to December 1875 said he would meet Mace on Mace's terms, denied putting up a forfeit, and said he had not heard from Mace officially.
Tom Allen was reported to have said Jem Mace would fight him for $10 or as much as Mace could raise, after Allen's 1876 fight with Joe Goss, when Allen went to Chicago and spoke to Mike McDonald.
Tom Allen was said to want a rematch with Johnny Dwyer to reverse his earlier defeat.
Steve Taylor said he was ready to fight Tom Allen at catch weight under London prize ring rules for $1,000 a side within 500 miles of New York the next April.
Tom Allen and Jem Mace traded statements in early 1876 over whether Mace would come to America to fight Allen for the championship.
Tom Allen offered to back Theobald Bauer to wrestle Andre Christol, and Christol replied he would wrestle only in Chicago, not St. Louis.
A fight between Joe Goss and Tom Allen was reported as expected or being arranged in late April and early May 1876.
Tom Allen offered to fight Joe Coburn with gloves for all the money Coburn could raise, or for nothing, and would back his offer with a $500 bet.
Joe Goss arrived from England in New York in April 1876 to make a match with Tom Allen for the championship, and planned to go to St. Louis to challenge him formally.
Joe Coburn refused Tom Allen's offer to fight with gloves, calling it an advertising dodge, and left for New York on April 24, 1876 promising to return with Jem Mace and Joe Goss.
Joe Goss and Tom Allen each put up a $500 forfeit with Eph Holland at Cincinnati, Holland acting as stakeholder, as the fight arrangements went ahead.
Joe Goss challenged Tom Allen for the championship in 1876 and Allen promptly accepted.
Tom Allen and Joe Goss were to meet at Cincinnati on 12 May 1876 to draw up articles for their fight, and Goss said Allen had authorized William Allen of Cincinnati to make the match.
Tom Allen and Joe Goss signed articles for their fight for the championship of the world at Cincinnati on 12 May 1876, at Eph Holland's Empire Saloon.
Red Leary offered to let the fight go on for a fresh stake of $1,000 a side, and Tom Allen declined, saying he could not have fair play.
Ben Hogan challenged Tom Allen by letter to fight in Canada to show who was the better man, offering to pay Allen's expenses to Detroit or to fight for stakes.
The Globe-Democrat sporting column headed its notice of Tom Allen 'Tom Allen Again Matched' in December 1877.
Tom Allen and Jack Knifton of Manchester were matched for £200 a side and the championship of the world, to fight in England about four weeks later.
Tom Allen and Charley Davis were matched in early 1878 for £100 a side and the English championship, with forfeit money posted.
In November 1878 Johnny Minan of San Francisco offered to match an unknown fighter, said to be Tom Allen, for $1,000 or $2,000 a side against Paddy Ryan, Mike McCoole or others.
In May 1879 John Dwyer, after beating Jimmy Elliott, said he wanted to fight Tom Allen and offered a £10 forfeit to Bell's Life for a match.
In June 1879 Tom Allen of St. Louis agreed, conditionally, to accept John Dwyer's challenge for the championship of America, and said he would cover the $250 Dwyer posted with Frank Queen.

On November 20, 1879, Tom Allen, then in London, issued a challenge to fight John Dwyer or any man at catch weights for $1,000 a side, in Canada within 100 miles of Buffalo or within 50 miles of Pittsburg.
In May 1880 Alfred Greenfield, the English heavyweight, challenged Tom Allen for £200 or £500, or for a £1,000 champion trophy, and Allen posted a forfeit to meet him in a sixteen-foot ring.
In December 1880 Tom Allen said no would-be champion in England would take £50 or £100 and fight him for it.

In October 1882 Richard K. Fox posted $1,000 with Harry Hill and offered to back Tom Allen against John L. Sullivan or any other pugilist for the championship of the world, at $1,000 to $2,500 a side.
Mr. Harding, Tom Allen's representative, did not go to Harry Hill's theatre to settle the $1,000 match, and Farrell, a friend of John L. Sullivan, claimed the $1,000 that Fox had posted.
Richard K. Fox said he would match Jim Mace against John L. Sullivan only if Sullivan defeated Tom Allen.

On November 2, 1882, Tom Allen challenged John L. Sullivan, or any man in the world, to fight for the championship of the world under London prize ring rules, with a $1,000 deposit posted by his backer; Sullivan was notified and meetings were set to sign articles.

At his exhibition on November 27, 1882, John L. Sullivan said he had not come to make a match with Tom Allen and would not be permitted to spar with him, and a fight between them was then considered scarcely probable.

In December 1882 Tom Allen was to accept Jim Elliott's challenge for $1,000 and the American championship, but on December 14 he did not appear at Charles E. Davies' place in Chicago to sign articles, and Richard K. Fox dropped him.
George Morrow offered to bet $500 that Tom Allen could not knock out J. Miles in four three-minute rounds.
In March 1883 Mitchell challenged Slade, Sullivan, Jem Mace, Joe Goss or Tom Allen to meet him for $5,000 to $10,000 a side; the men named did not reply.

On September 30, 1886, Tom Allen challenged an unnamed man to meet Duncan C. Ross in a broadsword contest for $500 a side and deposited a $200 forfeit with the Post-Dispatch; Ross ignored the challenge, and Allen withdrew the forfeit in October because Ross had not covered it.

In February 1888 Tom Allen deposited $160 for Flint, which the McManus party covered, and took part in arranging a fight to a finish between Flint and McManus at 160 pounds under Queensberry rules, witnessing the signing of the articles.
On January 17, 1891, Jack King said he had $50 in Tom Allen's hands for a fight between Allen and Mike Boden and asked Allen to cover it and arrange a match.
On January 17, 1891, Jack King said Tom Allen had been talking about fighting anybody in St. Louis.
In November 1892 Tom Allen said he had told Dutch Niel he would give $50 toward a purse for Niel's contest with Johnnie Daly, and denied that he would furnish a $500 side bet.
In late 1893 Tom Allen wrote to Ed Smith advising him to try to arrange a match with Jackson.
Ed Smith wrote to Tom Allen, in a letter received December 22, 1893, that his next fight would be with the winner of the Corbett-Mitchell fight.
On January 11, 1895, Tom Allen announced he would back Al J. Neist against Mike Mooney in a lightweight wrestling match, any style, for $250 a side, winner take all.
In February 1895 Jem Mace said he wanted to come to America and fight Tom Allen again, after hearing that Allen had said he could whip him.
In June 1897 Tom Allen said he would back Denver Ed Smith if Smith could get a fight with a prominent pugilist or one of the big heavyweights.
